#2931. Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1255 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • According to recent reports, in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

According to recent reports, in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Recent findings suggest that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

In a recent development, we included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

In a recent development, falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

It has been revealed that the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

It has been revealed that falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

Recent findings suggest that we thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

It has been revealed that درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

According to recent reports, WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

Recent findings suggest that قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

Recent findings suggest that تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

Sources indicate that سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

In a recent development, ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

It has been revealed that يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

#2930. Symbolic Abstraction Refinement

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (351 w)

Symbolic Abstraction Refinement

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (351 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22404v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

arXiv:2611.22374v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally notes "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub challenges made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt notes: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

Sources indicate that you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Industry observers note that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

In a recent development, image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

According to recent reports, before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

It has been revealed that paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Industry observers note that training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

According to recent reports, it took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

In a recent development, I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

An notable challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device.
  • LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • In a recent development, pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

In a recent development, pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

Industry observers note that we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

In a recent development, serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

arXiv:2611.22309v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.

In a recent development, black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

In a recent development, boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Industry observers note that for edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

In a recent development, black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

According to recent reports, A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

It has been revealed that let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

In a recent development, the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

Industry observers note that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

It has been revealed that at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

According to recent reports, the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

It has been revealed that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

Sources indicate that the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are newly introduced to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

Recent findings suggest that get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (205 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

Industry News: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. This runtime, the agent harness, manages context and memory, steers multi-turn control, executes tool actions in sandboxes, and verifies work before stopping. Because models differ in how they use tools and how they fail, a static harness tuned for one model or task often stalls, wastes tokens, or regresses on another. This bottleneck has driven a shift from prompt tuning to self-improving agent harnesses: systems that inspect their own execution traces, separate runtime bugs from model limits, and rewrite their own code. We present a unifying architectural and design framework for self-improving agent harnesses. The framework pairs four editable runtime components (context and state, agent control, action interfaces, and verification and recovery) with a four-stage loop that diagnoses failures, proposes code patches, validates candidates, and deploys updates. Using this framework, we show how optimizers trace errors across long trajectories and discover reusable runtime mechanisms such as pre-stop verifiers, loop breakers, and persistent memory. We further show why full-harness rewrites overfit or break across modules, and how modular updates with validation gates generalize across models while bounding token cost. To keep self-modification safe, we establish practical defenses against recurring failure modes including prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering. Finally, experiments on SWE-bench Lite validate this framework, showing that gated modular evolution outperforms prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites across models and repositories at a fraction of the token cost.

Streaming On-Policy Distillation: Decoupling Three Clocks for Stage-Wise Supervision Consumption

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In on-policy distillation (OPD), response completion, supervision delivery, and parameter updates need not share the same granularity. We develop streaming OPD by decoupling these three clocks: a response repeatedly delivers newly generated segments while generation continues, retaining the full causal prefix at each delivery and computing loss only on new positions. A consumption protocol then organizes supervision budgets, position selection, staleness handling, and update scheduling, allowing control over quantity, coverage, and version lag across training stages. In GSM8K experiments distilling Qwen3-4B into Qwen3-0.6B with VERL, supervised-budget matching reduces the early gap between best test accuracies over seven common candidates from 4.55 to 2.42 points. Synchronous continuation from the same checkpoint reaches 73.39% best test accuracy over seven common candidates at u=384,...,576, versus 74.30% synchronous and 71.95% budget-matched (differences -0.91 and -2.35 points); an unpaired extended record reaches 76.12%. Freshness filtering and disagreement-overlap selection improve local peaks but do not establish sustained advantages. A system prototype reveals lower data-supply waiting times without establishing an equal-update speedup. Quality recovery and supply-side benefits are assessed separately; end-to-end gains must account for continuation cost.

#2910. Breaking: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📖 Baca

Breaking: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post demonstrates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that looks, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the fresh modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

According to recent reports, the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Sources indicate that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

In a recent development, muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

It has been revealed that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

It has been revealed that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Sources indicate that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

Industry observers note that as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

In a recent development, the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

In a recent development, you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section demonstrates how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Recent findings suggest that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Sources indicate that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

According to recent reports, now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

In a recent development, we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

Recent findings suggest that we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

In a recent development, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

It has been revealed that hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Recent findings suggest that you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

arXiv:2611.22296v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

arXiv:2611.22286v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All upcoming data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Recent findings suggest that alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

Industry observers note that while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the fresh release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 highlights strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

It has been revealed that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Recent findings suggest that proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been revealed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Sources indicate that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

It has been revealed that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (271 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22283v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.
