#2851. Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3869 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints.
  • According to recent reports, here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text.
  • Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.

According to recent reports, here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series, we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache.

Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases:.

It has been revealed that the cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm.

Sources indicate that A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength, every fresh turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength.

In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints.

KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.

It has been revealed that when you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match.

Sources indicate that the endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an patch replaces instances, the upcoming instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time.

According to recent reports, figure 1: KV-aware routing on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The router looks up the managed cache index and forwards the request to the instance that holds the longest cached match. Each instance reports KV cache events back to the index.

Recent findings suggest that in Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect.

With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration.

In a recent development, both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container.

We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

According to recent reports, in our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

In a recent development, before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice.

It has been revealed that if the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint. These fallbacks aren’t reported in the SageMaker AI console or metrics at launch, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working to confirm that routing is effective for your traffic.

With very short prompts there is less prefill to save, so prefix-aware routing can be all you need.

Recent findings suggest that prefix-aware routing needs no changes to your container, but it can’t see what an instance actually holds. KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise. It pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse and that cache is under pressure: long prompts, high load, and instances that run short of GPU memory for the KV cache. When that happens, the container evicts the least recently used parts of the cache, including parts of shared prompts and conversation history.

In a recent development, for example, a support assistant runs on three instances, and each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt. Conversation 1 starts on instance A, which caches the excerpt. Traffic rises, A runs short of memory, and the container evicts most of that excerpt. Instance B recently served another conversation over the same excerpt and still holds its first 4,000 tokens. When the next turn of conversation 1 arrives, prefix-aware routing sends it to A again, and A recomputes the excerpt. With KV-aware routing, A’s container has already reported the eviction, so the index indicates that B holds the longest match, and the request goes to B, which recomputes only the remaining tokens. At low load, A wouldn’t have evicted anything, and both strategies would have sent the request to A with the cache intact.

KV-aware routing helps most when requests reuse cached context in ways a fixed-length prefix can’t capture:.

According to recent reports, multi-turn conversations: Each turn sends the full conversation history, so the cached prefix grows with every turn. KV-aware routing matches the whole cached history and keeps each conversation on the instance that holds it. This matters most for long conversations. After the managed cache index reflects an eviction, the router doesn’t keep sending the conversation to an instance that has already dropped its cache.

According to recent reports, high-throughput inference with shared context: RAG applications prepend retrieved documents, and assistants send long system prompts with every request. KV-aware routing fits when these prompts are long and instances are under memory pressure. With a stable shared prefix and moderate load, prefix-aware routing also fits. Put the shared content first and in the same order: if the same documents appear in a different order, the prompts no longer share a start, so they don’t match.

According to recent reports, workloads where prefix length is hard to tune: With prefix-aware routing, you choose a PrefixLength that covers your shared text without scattering requests that should stay together. KV-aware routing has no prefix length to tune, because it matches on what is actually cached.

Prefix-aware routing is a good fit, with no container changes, if your requests share a stable system prompt or document at the start, your prompts are short, or load is moderate. In these cases, instances have enough GPU memory to keep the shared text cached, so both strategies find it. Prefix-aware routing is also the choice if your container isn’t supported by KV-aware routing, because it works with any container that has prefix caching turned on. If your requests are short and interchangeable, or your model isn’t an LLM, there is little cached context to reuse, so use RANDOM or LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS.

If you aren’t sure which fits, start with prefix-aware routing, run your own traffic against a KV_AWARE endpoint, and compare time to first token, throughput, and hit rate as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Before you enable KV-aware routing, check that your container, endpoint, and requests meet these requirements:.

Recent findings suggest that container: At launch, KV-aware routing supports the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container for SageMaker AI: images with vLLM 0.33.0 or later, or the Amazon Linux build server-sagemaker-cuda-v2.8.0 or later. Prefix caching must be on, which is the default, and KV cache events must be turned on with the SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG environment variable, as shown in How to enable it. SageMaker AI doesn’t set it for you.

Endpoints and instances: Real-time single model endpoints and inference component endpoints, including dynamic Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, on GPU instance types. You can also configure KV-aware routing with AWS CloudFormation. Routing is active only with at least two instances for a single model endpoint, or at least two copies of an inference component, which can be on the same instance. With fewer, you can still set KV_AWARE and the endpoint isn’t rejected, but every request goes to the single instance or copy.

In a recent development, requests: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions payloads, sent with InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, or the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream isn’t supported. If you set the model field, it must match the value of SM_VLLM_MODEL.

SDK versions: Detailed observability, which you use to track the KV cache hit rate, needs AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2.35.6 or later, or Boto3 version 1.43.31 or later.

Sources indicate that sageMaker AI checks these requirements before your endpoint serves traffic. If a check fails, the request or deployment fails with a message that describes what is missing. For the full list of settings, validation behavior, and quotas, see the SageMaker AI documentation.

Sources indicate that you turn on KV-aware routing in two places: the model and the endpoint configuration. The example notebook runs every step end to end, for both a single model endpoint and an inference component endpoint.

According to recent reports, 1. Turn on KV cache events in the model – When you create the model, add SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG to the container environment. Without it, the endpoint has no cache state to route on. The ports in this setting are used only inside the instance, so you don’t open them to your network.

In a recent development, 2. Choose KV-aware routing in the endpoint configuration – Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the RoutingConfig of the production variant:.

If your container image is built for CUDA 13, also set InferenceAmiVersion in the production variant to an AMI that supports it, such as al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1. Otherwise the container can fail to start. See Inference GPU drivers.

Check that your account has enough endpoint quota for the instance type and count you choose, and request an increase in Service Quotas if needed.

The same RoutingConfig setting works for inference component endpoints, including dynamic LoRA adapters. For adapters, KV-aware routing chooses among the instances that already have the adapter loaded.

It has been revealed that nothing changes in how you call the endpoint. Send a Chat Completions payload with InvokeEndpoint, or with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream and "stream": true in the request body:.

You can also call the endpoint with the OpenAI Python client through the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. The Use the OpenAI-compatible API with SageMaker AI notebook on GitHub shows how, for both single model endpoints and inference components.

KV-aware routing doesn’t apply the multi-tenant prefix isolation from part 1: it ignores the prefix-aware ID header and the prompt_cache_key field. A request that sets a top-level cache_salt field to a non-null value is rejected with a 400 error.

In a recent development, KV-aware routing adds two error cases: a request whose model field names a model that the container doesn’t serve fails with a ModelError, and a request with a non-null cache_salt is rejected with a 400 error. Errors from inference itself are returned as before, and your model container’s own logs in Amazon CloudWatch can help you find the cause. The endpoint doesn’t deliver logs about its KV-aware routing decisions to your account, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working, such as cached_tokens per request and the KV cache hit rate, to see how routing behaves.

KV-aware routing doesn’t add metrics of its own, so you check its effect on your model. There are three ways to do this.

Check cache hits per request – The container doesn’t report prompt token details by default, so set SM_VLLM_ENABLE_PROMPT_TOKENS_DETAILS to true in the model environment. Each response then includes usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, the number of prompt tokens that were served from the KV cache. When you send a follow-up turn, or another request that starts the same way as an earlier one, a non-zero value demonstrates that the request reached an instance that held its prefix.

It has been revealed that check model metrics in Amazon CloudWatch – Turn on detailed observability by adding --metrics-config '{"EnableDetailedObservability": true}' when you create the endpoint configuration, using the SDK versions in Requirements and limits. SageMaker AI then publishes the model container’s metrics, including the KV cache hit rate and TTFT. Query them as described in Detailed observability with PromQL.

Sources indicate that figure 2: Verifying KV-aware routing. (a) A follow-up request reveals most prompt tokens served from the KV cache. (b) The KV cache hit rate for the same endpoint in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard.

Compare with the strategy you would otherwise use – For most LLM workloads the real choice is between KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE, so compare those two, and add a RANDOM endpoint as a baseline. Use the same model, instance type, and instance count for each endpoint, and send the same prompts at the same concurrency for the same duration, so that the only difference is the routing strategy. Make sure your test reuses context the way your production traffic does, for example with multi-turn conversations or shared documents. If KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE perform about the same for your traffic, prefix-aware routing is the simpler choice.

Sources indicate that as an example of this comparison, we compared RANDOM and KV_AWARE on a small endpoint. We sent the same multi-turn workload to two endpoints that differ only in routing strategy. Each endpoint had two ml.g5.xlarge instances serving Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on a supported container. Each run sent 128 requests: 32 simulated users, each asking 4 questions about a document chosen from 12 documents of about 7,400 tokens. Each question resends the conversation so far, so every question after the first can reuse cached context. We ran two pairs of runs, with RANDOM first in pair 1 and KV_AWARE first in pair 2, and used upcoming documents for each pair so that both endpoints started with empty caches. Table 1 demonstrates the results as pair 1 / pair 2.

In a recent development, table 1: RANDOM and KV_AWARE routing under the same workload. Each cell demonstrates pair 1 / pair 2. ModelLatency and OverheadLatency are Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the endpoint. The client measured time to first token and run duration. The cache share is the sum of cached_tokens divided by the sum of prompt_tokens over a run.

In both pairs, KV_AWARE had lower CloudWatch ModelLatency (average 1,235 and 1,314 ms against 4,124 and 5,100 ms) and lower time to first token for questions 2–4 (p50 237 and 245 ms against 1,284 and 1,632 ms). Its cache share was higher, at 90 percent in both pairs against 76 and 70 percent. OverheadLatency, the time SageMaker AI spends outside the model container, was 14 to 19 ms higher on average with KV_AWARE. This is one model, one instance type, and one workload with long shared documents, so measure your own traffic as described earlier in this section. Figure 3 shows the model latency charts that the SageMaker AI console displays for the two endpoints.

According to recent reports, figure 3: One-minute average model latency in Amazon CloudWatch for the RANDOM endpoint (blue) and the KV_AWARE endpoint (orange), on a shared 0–7 second axis. Each endpoint received seven consecutive runs of the same workload on latest documents, RANDOM first. Average model latency was 4.9–6.2 seconds for RANDOM and 1.2–1.3 seconds for KV_AWARE. The last RANDOM point is lower because that minute holds only the last 20 requests of the run.

If neither does better than RANDOM, check that prefix caching and KV cache events are turned on in the container, as described in Requirements and limits.

The example notebook applies the steps in this post to Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on two ml.g5.xlarge instances, the minimum for a single model endpoint, and on an inference component endpoint with two copies. It calls the endpoint with both APIs, reveals in the container logs that follow-up requests are served from the KV cache, and doesn’t compare routing strategies. Run its cleanup cells at the end to avoid ongoing charges.

Industry observers note that to avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created. For an inference component endpoint, delete the inference components first (delete-inference-component), then the endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model (delete-endpoint, delete-endpoint-config, delete-model).

These three practices help you keep KV-aware routing effective after you turn it on.

Monitor the KV cache hit rate – Keep detailed observability on after launch and watch the KV cache hit rate over time in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard (Figure 2b), or query it with PromQL, as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

According to recent reports, strategy for cold starts – The first request with new context, such as a new document or the first turn of a conversation, has nothing cached on any instance. KV-aware routing speeds up the requests that follow, not the first one.

Initiative for cache rebuilds during scaling and updates – As described in How KV-aware routing works, fresh instances start with empty caches. To soften the latency increase, use a rolling or blue/green upgrade for single model endpoints, or a RollingUpdatePolicy for inference components.

Sources indicate that KV-aware routing gives SageMaker AI real-time endpoints a second way to send requests to where their prompts are cached. It uses the cache state that your model container reports, so it follows the cache when instances evict it under memory pressure. Prefix-aware routing from part 1 of this series remains the simpler choice for stable shared prompts, short contexts, and moderate load. SageMaker AI handles routing inside the endpoint for both strategies, so you don’t build or run a routing layer yourself. You turn it on with one environment variable in the model and "RoutingStrategy": "KV_AWARE" in the endpoint configuration.

KV-aware routing is available today in all commercial AWS Regions that support SageMaker AI real-time inference, for endpoints that use a supported container. It is available at no additional charge. SageMaker AI runs and manages the cache index for you, and you pay only for the instances your endpoint uses. KV_AWARE is a fresh value for the existing RoutingStrategy field, so you don’t need a new configuration object, and older versions of the AWS CLI and Boto3 accept it. To get started, read the documentation, run the example notebook on a small endpoint, and then compare KV_AWARE with PREFIX_AWARE on a copy of your own traffic.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.18660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For an insurance portfolio modelled by a large number of i.i.d. losses, the average loss converges to its expected value by the law of large numbers, reflecting the diversification effect of pooling risks. Policy cancellations reduce the portfolio size and thereby weaken this effect. We quantify the resulting increase in risk by applying risk measures to the average loss before and after the cancellation of policies. For a portfolio of size $n$, we show that the impact of cancelling a single contract is of order $n^{-3/2}$, while the cancellation of a fixed proportion of contracts has an effect of order $n^{-1/2}$. We further extend the proportional cancellation regime to heterogeneous portfolios with different cancellation rates and risk characteristics across segments. These asymptotic results provide a quantitative basis for assessing surrender fees and cancellation costs from the insurer's perspective. We complement the theoretical analysis with numerical results for representative life insurance products, illustrating the magnitude of cancellation costs and the effect of portfolio aggregation. The two regimes require different techniques. For the cancellation of a fixed proportion of contracts, we employ central limit theorems in Wasserstein distance. For the cancellation of a single contract, we combine Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality with higher-order distributional approximations based on the Edgeworth and Cornish-Fisher expansions.

arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super key for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Sources indicate that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

According to recent reports, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

In a recent development, for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

According to recent reports, on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Industry observers note that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing demonstrated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

According to recent reports, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

arXiv:2611.22017v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, at the moment in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

Industry News: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all.
  • The pattern usually starts in a prototype.
  • At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.

The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost.

At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:.

It has been revealed that each fresh model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked.

Sources indicate that cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens, often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all?

Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements:.

If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model.

Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one.

According to recent reports, consider a customer support assistant. The following table reveals how five of its steps go through the chart.

You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table demonstrates what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model.

A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance.

Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation. On AWS, you can build it four ways:.

In a recent development, the following JSON schema limits a structured-output answer to four queues plus ‘unsure’. Amazon Bedrock requires every object in the schema to set additionalProperties to false.

Recent findings suggest that whichever option you choose, check its escalation signal against your own labeled data, and set any threshold there. Keep your authorization decisions, such as a refund limit, in a rule.

Many cost patterns focus on routing between models. The fast path goes one level earlier: Run the deterministic check first, and send only what the rule can’t settle to a model. Intent routing is one example. Many messages carry an unambiguous signal, such as “refund” or “reset my password”, which a keyword match resolves in single-digit milliseconds or less. If rules resolve 95 percent of requests, only 1 in 20 requests reaches a model, before any savings from model selection. (Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark.).

On AWS, you compose this from existing building blocks:.

Industry observers note that the following Choice state is a keyword fast path. It uses JSONata to send refund and password-reset messages straight to code, and it sends everything else to the constrained decision call.

Industry observers note that you can also let a model write the rule once instead of running it every time. Have it draft a regular expression or a JSON schema, review it, and commit it. At runtime the rule runs at rule speed and cost. Review a model-written regular expression, and test it against known good and bad inputs. Avoid nested quantifiers such as (a+)+, which can make matching very slow on some inputs (regular expression denial of service, or ReDoS).

Sources indicate that when you do generate, Amazon Bedrock structured outputs constrain a response to a JSON schema that you define. The response then matches the schema, so your code can parse it without custom parsing logic (check content for correctness). Keep range checks, such as numeric bounds and length limits, in code. For supported models and schema features, refer to Get validated JSON results from models.

If your rules live in configuration, allow only known primitives, such as regular expressions, schema checks, keyword lists, and range checks. Never run arbitrary code from a configuration file.

Industry observers note that choose the cheapest and fastest model that meets your quality floor. That is often not the newest or largest model. The Generative AI Lens covers this in its best practice on right-sizing model selection. Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock covers it in depth. Define the requirements before you compare models:.

In a recent development, amazon Bedrock offers many model families and sizes behind one API, so you can right-size each task without changing your integration. Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing routes each request to a suitable model within a supported model family. Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller, cheaper one for your use case. Model providers evaluate a new frontier model on broad benchmarks, but your workload is one task with one quality floor. A larger model can add cost and latency without improving that task. Before you switch, evaluate each launch against your requirements, such as quality on your golden evaluation set and your latency target.

Sources indicate that the Generative AI Lens recommends testing candidate models against your ground truth data and having a way to update the model quickly. Go further and treat the decision as a tested configuration:.

Spend model capacity where judgment is needed, and nowhere else. You can get there in four steps:.

It has been revealed that in this post, you learned how to decide whether a workflow step needs a model at all. Rules belong in deterministic code, and fixed choices belong in a constrained decision call. Open-ended work goes to a right-sized Amazon Bedrock model. Aim to meet each requirement at the lowest cost and latency that your quality floor allows. Ask whether a step needs a model before you ask which one.

For more information, refer to these posts on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog:.

To try a constrained decision call, open the Amazon Bedrock console, or deploy Strands Decider from its GitHub repository.

Start with one high-volume workflow and measure how much of it never needed a model.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

On Formal Counterfactual Explanations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Sources indicate that the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to proposal for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Recent findings suggest that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

Industry observers note that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Industry observers note that figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an crucial part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

In a recent development, publicly available genomic data has proved key in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

According to recent reports, making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

Sources indicate that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

It has been revealed that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Sources indicate that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

According to recent reports, teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

It has been revealed that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be confirmed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or firm building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

According to recent reports, we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (265 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21998v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (195 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2608.06618v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2607.04753v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Narratives often combine diagnostic evidence with truthful but nondiagnostic details. In a two-state experiment with known signal likelihoods, we test whether such details distort belief updating. Although Bayes' rule prescribes no revision, nondiagnostic signals induce revisions consistent with considering both states equally likely. Such revisions are most frequent when nondiagnostic signals appear as clues in a story, less frequent in an abstract urn problem, and virtually absent when the same story replaces these clues with explicit no-information messages. Simulations show that these revisions reduce belief accuracy and delay decisions, an effect communicators could exploit without lying.

Industry News: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience.
  • Recent findings suggest that flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines initiative and manage their crews, flights, and operations.
  • In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload.

Recent findings suggest that flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines initiative and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow:.

Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow.

In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for people to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph, an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2):.

Sources indicate that this is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results:.

Industry observers note that note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage.

We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) indicates how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result.

Figure 3: Overview of the three optimization strategies in one agent turn.

Recent findings suggest that at the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool(). At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail.

To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place:.

The companion code is available in this GitHub repository.

Sources indicate that our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight.

To support this, we introduced a dedicated persisted-state schema that keeps only lightweight fields and artifact references. The live graph state still includes parsed domain objects for tool execution, but persistence now writes a dehydrated form. At runtime, tools hydrate heavy payloads on demand using those references, instead of loading everything on every turn.

This PersistedState schema is what gets written to AgentCore Memory:.

The updated GraphState mirrors these references alongside the live domain objects:.

The dehydrate_state function strips heavy payloads from the live state and returns the lightweight persisted form along with the artifacts to upload:.

It has been revealed that rehydration reverses this process. When a session resumes, we rebuild the live graph state: deserialize LangChain messages, re-parse raw payloads into domain objects, and restore every reference key so later turns can locate their artifacts:.

Both dehydration and rehydration rely on the artifact store returning a consistent reference for each payload. Instead of minting a random key, we derive the reference from the payload itself. This approach, known as content addressing, serializes the JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, and uses the SHA-256 digest of those bytes as the reference.

The _content_hash helper produces a deterministic SHA-256 reference from a JSON-serializable payload:.

Content addressing makes writes idempotent. Identical payloads map to the same key, so a turn that re-serializes an unchanged request JSON reuses the object already in the bucket instead of uploading it again. The S3-backed store exposes a put_json and get_json interface. It also keeps a small in-process cache, so payloads already read or written during the current invocation do not require a second S3 round trip.

The S3ArtifactStore class wraps the put_json/get_json interface with an in-process cache and content-addressed keys:.

Offloading heavy artifacts to S3 and persisting only lightweight references reduced per-turn latency and the volume of data stored in AgentCore memory. With heavy payloads no longer persisted inline, tool-call responses became the dominant consumer of context tokens, prompting us to introduce result paging.

It has been revealed that even after moving heavy payload persistence to Amazon S3, we still had a major token bottleneck at tool-response time. Many tool results were too large, which created two problems. First, we were sending full lists to the model even when it only needed a small subset, making each turn slower and more expensive. Second, those full list payloads were injected into context, which rapidly consumed the context window over multi-turn conversations.

In some cases, a single tool response exceeded 80,000 tokens, and the cost compounded as consumers continued interacting with the agent. We wanted to preserve full data access without sending everything by default. To solve this, we introduced on-demand result paging for large tool outputs. Instead of returning full lists, tools now return a compact payload with total count, a small sample, and a result handle.

When a tool result exceeds the sample-size threshold, the full list is stored in S3 and only a compact summary is returned to the model:.

Sources indicate that the handle points to the complete result stored in S3. When the agent needs more detail, it calls a paging tool with the handle and requests only the required slice, for example using offset and limit.

The get_result_page_tool function lets the model retrieve additional slices of a stored result by handle, offset, and limit:.

On-demand paging kept the full list in S3 and served only the requested slice per turn, controlling context growth and significantly reducing token usage. However, not all oversized outputs were lists. Some tools returned large dictionaries that required a different compaction approach.

Sources indicate that unlike lists, dictionary outputs contain deeply nested structured data that are useful for reasoning but typically too expensive to include verbatim on each turn. We needed a compact representation that preserved structural cues while drastically cutting the token footprint.

According to recent reports, to solve this, we introduced descriptor-based compaction for oversized dictionary outputs. Instead of returning an oversized dictionary in full, we return a compact descriptor:.

Recent findings suggest that the full payload is stored in the artifact store, and the response includes a result handle. When the agent needs deeper detail, it uses that handle to fetch only the required data. This response format remained navigable for the model while significantly reducing unnecessary token usage.

The _oversized_descriptor function builds a compact structural summary of a dictionary payload, preserving field types and sample data without the full content:.

If the serialized output still exceeds the character limit, the fallback stores the full payload and replaces the response with its descriptor:.

With lightweight persisted state, on-demand paging, and dictionary compaction in place, token growth became predictable and the agent stayed responsive even on multi-megabyte datasets.

To validate the impact of these three strategies, we ran the same set of questions over the same dataset against both the pre-optimization and optimized versions of the agent. We then compared token usage and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability (a capability of AgentCore), and observed clear improvements in both cost and responsiveness.

Across a 5-question conversation run, total token usage dropped by approximately 71%, from ~289,500 to ~82,900 tokens, while average trace latency decreased by nearly 80%, from 15.4 s to 3.1 s (Figure 4). Across 100 sample questions (Figure 5), total tokens fell from 23.6 M to 8.5 M (64%) and average trace latency dropped from 7,930 ms to 2,461 ms (69%).

Figure 4: OTEL sessions comparison.

Figure 5: OTEL sessions comparison across 100 sample questions.

According to recent reports, the effect was most dramatic on large single-turn payloads. Table 1 breaks down the per-turn impact for the heaviest single query (listing valid crews across every validation category).

Table 1: Input, output, and latency impact.

Figure 6 and Figure 7 show the corresponding trace details before and after optimization.

In a recent development, these gains came primarily from avoiding full payload injection into model context at every turn. Instead, the model now receives compact summaries first and fetches additional detail only when needed.

Figure 8: Compact summary event.

The improvement was also visible in the trace timelines: the pre-optimization turn stretched to nearly 2 minutes 46 seconds, while the optimized turn completed in about 15 seconds (Figure 9).

Figure 9: Before and after timeline.

The changes also improved behavior in longer conversations. Context growth became more predictable across turns, and the agent remained responsive even when users asked follow-up questions over large datasets. In practice, this shifted the system from compounding token cost to a more controlled, demand-driven access pattern.

Recent findings suggest that most importantly, these gains came without sacrificing capability. Full payloads remain in artifact storage and can be retrieved through handles whenever deeper inspection is needed. At Flightscape, this pattern provides a foundation for bringing conversational AI capabilities to complex airline operations workflows, keeping the underlying AI experience scalable and cost efficient.

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created for this walkthrough:.

If your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent handles large JSON data, start by identifying which tool outputs dominate your context window. Begin with offloading artifacts to S3 (Strategy 1) because it provides the foundation for the other optimizations, then add paging (Strategy 2) and compaction (Strategy 3) as needed to improve the token usage and latency of your agents. To get started, clone the GitHub repository and adapt the strategies to your own agent. To learn more about building agents with AgentCore and LangGraph, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the LangGraph framework documentation.

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding latest expertise on a single endpoint.

Industry observers note that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

In a recent development, while we are excited about these latest features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this patch. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

arXiv:2611.21950v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

In the cryptocurrency ecosystem, lending and staking yields are predominantly variable and adjust over short timescales, whereas fixed-rate instruments remain scarce and, as of early 2026, widely accepted benchmark yield curves were still lacking.
