Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation.
  • Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo, combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges.
  • The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo, combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod.

The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components:.

AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, revision the add-on.

Sources indicate that the following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA.

Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview.

It has been revealed that hyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints.

Figure 1: Deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference.

Whether you are newly introduced to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow:.

Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster.

In a recent development, inferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference people deploy a new Dynamo endpoint using the same configuration format and OpenAI-compatible interface they already know. For the inference engine, you can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts.

In a recent development, both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. In either case, HyperPod manages node health and replacement. The table summarizes the responsibilities for each path.

In a recent development, the following excerpts use the InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) deployment path with vLLM on ml.p5.48xlarge instances. Dynamo-specific settings belong under spec.dynamoSpec. Model source and endpoint settings are included in the complete manifest.

Recent findings suggest that this configuration runs one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs), with two frontend replicas for request handling. Setting dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode to kv-aware turns on KV-aware routing.

Here, spec.replicas controls the number of model-worker replicas, while frontend.replicas controls the number of frontend replicas.

Industry observers note that replace aggregation under spec.dynamoSpec with the following disaggregation block, keeping the preceding frontend configuration. Replica counts are set separately for prefill and decode. This example runs one prefill replica and two decode replicas, each spanning two instances, for a total of six instances.

Recent findings suggest that apply the complete manifest with kubectl apply. The HyperPod Inference Operator makes the configured model weights available to the workers and generates the DGD. Grove and KAI Scheduler coordinate placement so that the pods required for each multi-node worker are scheduled together.

After the SageMaker endpoint is ready and configured for chat completions, clients can send an OpenAI-compatible request payload through the SageMaker Runtime API:.

We benchmarked Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod across two models to compare serving configurations.

We used AIPerf to compare aggregated and disaggregated serving for Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 using Dynamo with TensorRT-LLM on two p5en.48xlarge instances (16 H200 GPUs). Requests contained 4,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens. We retained measured points that met two targets: P90 time to first token below one second, and median generation speed of at least 50 tokens per second per user. Among these points, disaggregated serving achieved 2.05× the highest aggregated throughput: 207 versus 101 output tokens per second per GPU, at concurrency 80 and 32, respectively.

Figure 2: Aggregated compared to disaggregated serving throughput for Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8.

Dynamo supports multi-node serving in both aggregated and disaggregated modes for models that exceed a single instance’s GPU memory. To evaluate a worker spanning nodes, we used AIPerf to benchmark multi-node aggregated serving for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 with Dynamo and vLLM, using TP4 × PP2 and eight active H200 GPUs. This model fits on one instance, so in practice you would not split it. It serves here as a controlled baseline. We compared eight GPUs on one p5en.48xlarge against four GPUs on each of two instances, using the same model, parallelism, and workload configuration. With an agentic workload featuring high prefix reuse at concurrency 32, the two-node configuration delivered 126.4 output tokens per second per GPU, retaining 99.1 percent of single-node throughput. This reveals that Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod can serve a model that needs more than one instance across nodes. The node boundary itself does not become a significant throughput penalty.

Figure 3: Single-node compared to two-node throughput for multi-node aggregated serving of Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8.

NVIDIA Dynamo provides recipes and tools to help you select a serving configuration, benchmark performance, and tune your deployment on SageMaker HyperPod.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod Inference simplifies deploying and operating large models with multi-node serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. The managed add-on installs the serving components, and configuration defaults simplify endpoint setup. HyperPod manages model weights, auto-scales clusters based on GPU and inference metrics, monitors node health, and replaces failed nodes. Together, these capabilities reduce undifferentiated infrastructure work so teams can focus on their models and applications. Get started with the setup instructions and complete deployment examples in the linked repository.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (267 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.21948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Concern Advocate or an Honest Broker. These findings on the supply of evidence in public comments shed light on an often overlooked form of policymaking that has implications for how and through what sources information is made accessible to regulators of AI.

Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

Latest Update: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Sources indicate that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is substantial: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Sources indicate that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is substantial: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

According to recent reports, the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

It has been revealed that our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

It has been revealed that model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

In a recent development, A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

Sources indicate that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

Sources indicate that it also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

It has been revealed that A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

Recent findings suggest that one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

According to recent reports, we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

Industry observers note that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

Recent findings suggest that we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

Sources indicate that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a significant model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

According to recent reports, it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

In a recent development, with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

In a recent development, so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

Industry observers note that the Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

t5/umt5 in a blog post in 2026, never thought I’d see the day 😍.

arXiv:2611.24714v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (239 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21946v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework states what to measure before building a stopping rule.

arXiv:2611.24659v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.

arXiv:2611.21937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Sources indicate that every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Recent findings suggest that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where fresh models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Recent findings suggest that of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#2810. Breaking: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1338 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at Exa, we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources.
  • This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware (AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization.
  • Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at Exa, we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. We optimize the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. We use multi-tower semantic machine learning (ML) models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space, so users can express complex queries in natural language alongside traditional keyword search. The keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database. It must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. The unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything we do. At the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding the hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar isn’t a tuning detail. Any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number.

This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware (AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization.

Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving.

Figure 1: A simplified view of the Exa stack.

Every structured web document we rank as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. This figure shows how raw web data moves from Crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of Parse, Moderate and filter, then Embed, with the result served from a vector database.

In a recent development, our experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding our existing corpus. We selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. A migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate our hardware choices.

Figure 2: The doubled inference load from the backfill.

Recent findings suggest that the preceding figure shows two parallel pipelines sharing the crawl and parse stages, one embedding with the live model into the live index and one re-embedding priority documents with the newly introduced model into the new index, which is what doubles the load. This doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider our hardware and optimization choices.

AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance (inf2.xlarge), with one chip and two NeuronCores. Our workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so we run Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving us container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. The same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Our initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model. From that baseline, it became a march to push throughput (docs/sec) as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. The following chart reveals the throughput gains at each milestone.

Figure 3: Throughput improvement across optimization milestones.

It has been revealed that starting from the naive compile, a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement. The first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. We also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. The downcast outputs met our correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference (see Agentic methodology), so the accuracy impact was within our acceptance threshold.

The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. These pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and we used them to promptly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. A drop-in attention kernel gave us the next bump in performance.

Recent findings suggest that the next bottleneck was memory spill. Profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently indicated large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Using a drop-in MLP kernel as a steppingstone to profile the shortcomings of the pre-built implementation, we wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls.

We used the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops, and memory operations, and only dropped into the lower-level NKI ISA for specific tensor operations. Keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers, and easier to debug.

In a recent development, at this point we hit a wall. Per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what we saw with both cores running simultaneously. That gap meant our theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above our realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores.

Recent findings suggest that profiling and experimentation demonstrated that our workload wasn’t yet saturating the Tensor Engine. The remaining headroom was ours to claim by making the computation leaner. The clearest path left was to reduce the overall FLOPS needed to produce our results by eliminating waste. We rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in our model to cut FLOPS spent on padding. This is where kernel customization really paid off. Generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they can’t take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. We wrung more performance out of attention by tailoring the implementation to the real shape of our model’s head architecture. We also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. That cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup.

In total, our final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against our initial baseline.

Agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction. Using Flyte, an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. The workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. It then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware.

Sources indicate that the harness supports agents at different costs. Lightweight models handle tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters, and correctness checks prevent drift. Reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them. Matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Because many agents don’t know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped.

So far, we have optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service.

Industry observers note that exa schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Our scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts. Each hardware type we optimize for brings us closer to the global optimum. This is why our Inferentia2 work carried over directly to Trainium2. Shifting hardware profiles lets us free up nodes other teams need or absorb their unused reserved compute. For a long lived model, optimizing across hardware pays off enormously.

At the scale Exa operates, extracting maximum cost-performance from a flexible pool of hardware is what matters. Adding Neuron hardware to that pool and optimizing it with NKI has proven to be a major source of long-term cost savings.

Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.24028v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever fresh information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.21925v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these problems, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (331 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21885v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

#2803. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Industry observers note that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Industry observers note that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer intends the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

In a recent development, it makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide states and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

It has been revealed that nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one notes, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

In a recent development, each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

Sources indicate that we trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

According to recent reports, there's no public corpus of prepares, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and indicates why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

In a recent development, "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

Sources indicate that "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Owners often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the strategy and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

Industry observers note that the designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

Industry observers note that the model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

According to recent reports, figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

According to recent reports, figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

Sources indicate that first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

Sources indicate that to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

In a recent development, we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a strategy, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

It has been revealed that the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

arXiv:2611.24266v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Real options (RO) modeling provides a powerful framework for valuing managerial flexibility under uncertainty in capital-intensive investments across various industries, including climate, energy, and transportation. However, the transparency and usefulness of such models depends heavily on sensitivity analysis (SA). This study reviews over 100 peer-reviewed RO journal articles to examine the extent and quality of SA practices. The review focuses particularly on the extent of model scrutiny: how many input variables are subjected to sensitivity analysis; whether local or global approaches are applied; and whether the shape of the input-output relationships is examined. Our findings reveal a strong overreliance on one-at-a-time (OAT) techniques and a corresponding minimal adoption of global sensitivity analysis (GSA). This methodological gap limits the ability of the RO field to critically examine its own models and to support its decision-making. The paper concludes by outlining concrete recommendations for how to effectively incorporate GSA into future RO studies in order to enhance model transparency, relevance, and credibility.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.21832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

#2799. Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2061 w)

Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a manufacturer’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone.
  • According to recent reports, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters.
  • Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a manufacturer’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone. For businesses, the value is twofold. A fine-tuned model delivers measurably better accuracy on domain-specific work while reducing costs: a smaller specialized model can match or exceed a frontier model on your task at a fraction of the per-token inference price. Those savings compound across millions of requests. Fine-tuning has therefore become an essential process for businesses looking to get more value from LLMs at lower costs.

According to recent reports, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters. LoRA aims to strike a balance between efficiency and expressiveness, however, the low-rank nature of the weight update inherently limits the representation power of LoRA fine-tuned models, potentially compromising performance on complex tasks. This trade-off hampers the ability of LoRA methods to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. To address these challenges, Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) updates model parameters simultaneously, overcoming the low-rank limitations so LLMs can fully absorb complex domain-specific knowledge.

Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure. There is no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration required. In this post, we explore when and where FFT consistently outperforms LoRA across key benchmarks, examine the spectral properties of model weight matrices that explain this quality gap, provide practical hyperparameter tuning guidelines backed by controlled experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and show you how to get started with FFT on SageMaker AI.

Model customization types like LoRA reduce trainable parameters by freezing the pre-trained model’s weights and injecting small, separate pairs of replacement matrices (called low-rank matrices) into the model layers. This works well for simple adaptations, but the low-rank structure inherently limits the representation power of the fine-tuned model. As tasks grow more complex and datasets scale beyond tens of thousands of examples, LoRA hits an accuracy plateau where increasing rank (and thus trainable parameters) fails to bridge the accuracy gap with standard fine-tuning. This plateau reveals that the performance gap isn’t simply because of fewer parameters. It’s caused by rank deficiency itself. The low-rank update can’t capture the full complexity of the weight changes needed for deep task adaptation.

According to recent reports, however, for complex tasks and domains where large, good-quality datasets exist, full-rank fine-tuning excels by updating model parameters simultaneously. FFT modifies the model’s weight matrix uniformly, using the full representational capacity of the model’s weight matrices rather than restricting updates to a small subspace, and without introducing the abrupt, localized distortions characteristic of low-rank methods. The result is stronger model convergence, better activation alignment across model layers, and a model that faithfully captures both the target task distribution and the richness of its pre-trained knowledge. FFT’s quality advantage grows with dataset scale: at 100K+ training examples, FFT achieved 90.0 percent on LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness across code generation tasks, as shown in the following chart.

Figure 1: LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness by training method as training data scales to 100K+ examples.

Furthermore, the following radar chart provides a holistic view: the base model (inner polygon) indicates consistently low scores across all axes. LoRA (middle polygon) shows strong, balanced improvement. FFT (outer polygon) extends further on every dimension, with particularly pronounced leads on BLEU and ROUGE-2 scores. This multi-dimensional quality lead confirms that it isn’t a metric-specific artifact but a fundamental advantage of full-rank optimization.

Figure 2: Radar chart comparing the base model, LoRA, and FFT across quality dimensions.

The details of how we arrived at these results, the coding datasets used for model customization, and the experimentation process are explained in detail in the following sections.

In a recent development, in this post we used the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) technique on a Qwen3-4B base model offered within Amazon SageMaker AI Studio and performed all the fine-tuning experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization across LoRA and FFT training methods. Within each experiment, both methods received the same prompts, targets, and evaluation code.

For all the experimentation, we fine-tuned the Qwen3-4B base model on the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset, a curated corpus of 110,000 coding instruction-response pairs spanning algorithm design, debugging, data structures, and systems programming. We applied a 90/5/5 split to the dataset: 99,000 records for training, 5,500 for validation to monitor convergence and training loss during the customization job, and 5,500 reserved as a held-out test set for unbiased evaluation of the final model, as registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets and shown in the following figure.

Figure 3: The 110K instruction-pair dataset registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets.

All the model customization experiments in this post were performed on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization. Serverless Model Customization on SageMaker AI lets data scientists and machine learning (ML) engineers focus on model fine-tuning without managing infrastructure or GPU capacity planning. You specify the base model, dataset, and hyperparameters, and the service handles compute allocation and checkpoint management automatically in a serverless fashion. The following code snippet demonstrates one such experiment for launching a Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) job on Serverless Model Customization using the SageMaker Python SDK.

The code triggers a serverless model customization job, shown in the following screenshot, with training performance metrics tracked in the job and viewable in the linked MLflow app.

Figure 4: Serverless model customization job with training metrics tracked in MLflow.

In a recent development, switching from Full Fine-Tuning to LoRA requires only one change: set TrainingType.FULL to TrainingType.LORA. The rest of the code remains identical:.

We tested the resulting customized models across three diverse evaluation methods built into SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization: LLM-as-Judge, PRIMECODE, and MMLU, shown in the following image. Each targets a different dimension of model quality: semantic correctness, code generation fidelity, and general knowledge retention. Together they provide a comprehensive picture of the model customization quality.

Figure 5: The three built-in evaluation methods in SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization.

The LLM-as-Judge metric uses a frontier model (in this post, Amazon Nova Pro) as an automated evaluator that reads the model’s generated code alongside the original prompt and judges whether the solution is logically correct. On serverless model customization you can evaluate both the customized model alongside the base model, as shown in the following figure.

Figure 6: LLM-as-Judge evaluation comparing the customized model and the base model.

PRIMECODE is a custom scorer evaluation that measures how closely the model’s generated code matches reference solutions using deterministic text-similarity metrics: BLEU (n-gram precision), ROUGE-1/2/L (recall-oriented overlap), and F1 (precision-recall balance). These metrics are fully reproducible, making them ideal for controlled ablation studies. We used PRIMECODE as our primary metric for surface-level code quality because it quantifies how well the model has learned the coding patterns, formatting conventions, and implementation style present in the training data. A high BLEU score means the model generates code that looks structurally similar to expert-written solutions, as shown in the following results.

Figure 7: PRIMECODE text-similarity scores for the customized model.

Industry observers note that MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is a built-in benchmark that tests the model across 57 academic subjects from abstract algebra and anatomy to Nutrition and Philosophy. It measures whether the model retains its broad general knowledge after domain-specific fine-tuning, as shown in the following figure. We used MMLU as our forgetting detection guardrail. Fine-tuning on code can overwrite general capabilities stored in the model’s weights. By tracking MMLU accuracy before and after fine-tuning, we can quantify exactly how much general knowledge the model sacrifices for code generation improvement, and whether our hyperparameter choices accelerate or mitigate this trade-off.

Figure 8: MMLU accuracy before and after fine-tuning.

It has been revealed that the ease of setup and use of SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization let us perform rapid experimentation without re-provisioning infrastructure. We changed training types between LoRA and FFT, swept hyperparameters, and tested across multiple base models. Over a short time window, we ran tens of model customization experiments across multiple supported base models (Qwen3-4B, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Nemotron-30B, Gemma-4-26B), systematically ablating learning rate, batch size, warmup ratio, epoch count, and dataset scale. Each experiment, from job submission to evaluation results, completed in a few hours and the resulting fine-tuned models were automatically registered in SageMaker Model Registry as versioned Model Packages, ready for review or deployment.

SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization supports many hyperparameters. In this section, we explain a few notable ones, informed by the series of experiments that we ran across multiple hyperparameter configurations within the previously mentioned code generation task. While effective values will vary by task, the patterns observed across these experiments provide useful starting points when configuring FFT model customization jobs. For more information about the hyperparameters that you can configure before launching an FFT model customization job, see the hyperparameters documentation page.

In full fine-tuning, the learning rate controls how aggressively every weight is updated. Unlike LoRA, where only small adapter matrices change, an FFT learning rate that is too high permanently overwrites pretrained knowledge. In our experiments, the following LR × dataset-size risk map demonstrates that an LR of 2e-5 on a large dataset (over 100 thousand) was the safe zone.

Figure 9: Learning rate and dataset-size risk map for full fine-tuning.

Sources indicate that epoch count in FFT is fundamentally a forgetting question, not a loss-curve question. Training loss will keep falling and your held-out validation will look healthy because it shares a distribution with training data, but capabilities on everything you didn’t train on quietly degrade. The LLM-as-Judge correctness score rose to 90.0 percent at 3 epochs, and extending beyond 3 epochs degraded every variant we experimented with.

Batch size determines how many examples contribute to each gradient step. At a fixed learning rate, smaller batches produce more noisy updates that behave much like a higher learning rate, increasing forgetting risk. Larger batches reduce noise but also reduce the number of optimization steps, potentially underfitting.

Figure 10: Effect of global batch size on model quality.

In a recent development, FFT modifies every parameter in the model, including the parameters that encode general knowledge acquired during pre-training. When fine-tuning pushes these parameters too aggressively toward a narrow domain, the model can “forget” its broader capabilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. We tested for this systematically using MMLU, measuring general knowledge retention across all our fine-tuning configurations. A baseline configuration with warmup=5 percent, batch size 8, and LR=2e-5 best preserved general knowledge (MMLU), as shown in the following figure.

Figure 11: MMLU general-knowledge retention across hyperparameter configurations.

In a recent development, hence, it is key to note that FFT isn’t universally superior to LoRA, and its effectiveness is extremely sensitive to hyperparameter choices. For example, in our experiments, both FFT and LoRA underperformed the base model on MATH exact match, underscoring the challenge of preserving reasoning capabilities during domain-specific fine-tuning. Aggressive learning rates (LR ≥ 5e-5) in FFT proved particularly destructive, causing MATH scores to plummet to 2–3 percent and MMLU accuracy to drop to 3.6 percent, clear evidence of catastrophic forgetting. Additionally, LoRA slightly outperformed FFT on the LLM-as-Judge metric (81.5 percent compared to 79.5 percent), demonstrating that parameter-efficient methods can still hold an edge on subjective quality assessments. These findings reinforce that the choice between FFT and LoRA should be guided by careful experimentation, dataset characteristics, and a clear understanding of the trade-offs involved.

In a recent development, with Full Fine-Tuning on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, your model can fully absorb domain-specific knowledge when task complexity and data scale demand it. If your use case requires deep adaptation, such as specialized reasoning, code generation, or domain-specific language understanding, and you have sufficient high-quality training data, FFT delivers measurably stronger results.

You can get started with FFT on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization with serverless training, built-in evaluation, and without infrastructure or compute capacity planning, so you can focus on your data and hyperparameter choices. You can use the SageMaker Python SDK to configure and launch your training and evaluation jobs programmatically. You can see the documentation for supported base models available for Full Fine-Tuning on Serverless Model Customization.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.23723v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: We study whether visually similar price histories predict similar future returns, using a vision model to retrieve each stock's most similar charts from three decades of U.S. price histories. A representation pretrained only on natural images already retrieves neighbors whose realized returns predict the cross-section of stock returns. Returns and order imbalances around portfolio formation indicate that the signal identifies temporary selling pressure that partially reverts. Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.21827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap, next to any accuracy figure. Code is public.
